冷.meaning: <part>Ice</part> chips rain down on a long queue while a grumpy clerk barks <part>orders</part> through the frost: 'Wait! Shuffle forward! Wait again!' Teeth chatter all down the line. It's <kanji>cool</kanji> in here.
冷.on: A <sound>ray</sound> slides by under the ice, cold and silent, and the clerk orders it to wait too.
冷.kun: The clerk's hands are so frozen he sneezes '<sound>Tsu</sound>!', drops his pen on a <sound>me</sound>tal tray, and his <sound>tie</sound> freezes stiff.

酒.meaning: <part>water drops</part> trickle onto a stick of <part>dynamite</part> packed with rice, and it sits for weeks in a dark shed. When the fuse finally blows, the drops have turned into something much stronger: <kanji>sake</kanji>, rice wine.
酒.on: The brewer tips in a big scoop of <sound>su</sound>gar to help it along.
酒.kun: The brewer packs a tin of <sound>sa</sound>rdines next to the dynamite and, at camp, warms the sake in a <sound>ke</sound>ttle.

皿.meaning: Seen from the side: a flat base, and on top a shallow tray split into sections by little walls, like a lunch tray. Pile food in each section: it's a <kanji>dish</kanji>.
皿.on: The dish is piled with shrimp, fresh from the boats in the <sound>bay</sound>.
皿.kun: A cheerleader leans over and licks a <sound>sa</sound>rdine off the dish: '<sound>Rah</sound>-rah!'

血.meaning: A <part>dish</part> sits on the table with one drop falling into it from above. Plink. A single red drop, then another, then another. Someone's finger is cut: it's <kanji>blood</kanji>.
血.on: At a picnic, a bat swoops down on your hotdog. It doesn't want blood after all: it licks off the <sound>ketch</sound>up and flies away.
血.kun: A <sound>chee</sound>tah scratches your arm, and this time the blood is real.

町.meaning: Next to a <part>rice field</part>, someone puts up a <part>street</part> sign and opens a hardware shop under it. Then come a baker, a school, a post office. The field has grown into a <kanji>town</kanji>.
町.on: The fanciest shop in town sells just one thing, a gold <sound>cho</sound>ker.
町.kun: The town's first shop sold only <sound>mu</sound>gs, and a <sound>chee</sound>tah ran the till.

又.meaning: Two strokes cross like a hand reaching out, palm down, to grab the last cookie. Caught? It grabs another. And another. Will it stop now, <kanji>or again</kanji>?
又.on: A <sound>u</sound>nicorn trots in and eats all the cookies again.
又.kun: '<sound>Ma</sound>! <sound>Ta</sound>-da!' the kid calls, holding up yet another cookie.

友.meaning: You can't steer the boat alone: the <part>rudder</part> is too stiff. A second hand reaches over and grips it with yours, fingers twisted together like a <part>pretzel</part>. Two hands, one boat, one course. That's a <kanji>friend</kanji>.
友.on: Your friend gallops up on a <sound>u</sound>nicorn and offers to row the rest of the way.
友.kun: Your friend carves both your faces on a <sound>to</sound>tem pole and wraps its foot in a soft <sound>mo</sound>ccasin.

支.meaning: A tree's longest arm sags under its apples. A gardener's hand, twisted tight like a <part>pretzel</part>, wedges a crossed stick shaped like a <part>ten</part> underneath. Stick holds arm, arm holds apples: one <kanji>branch</kanji> propped up by another.
支.on: When the stick cracks, the gardener jams a knight's <sound>shi</sound>eld under the branch instead.
支.kun: The propped branch holds a cat with a <sound>sa</sound>rdine in one paw and another <sound>sa</sound>rdine in the other, and it doesn't even bend.
